Maurene Comey var føderal anklager i New York, arbejdede på nogle af de mest profilerede sager i USA og fik 'de højeste anerkendelser fra både overordnede og kolleger'.
Men hun var også datter af en tidligere FBI-direktør, som Donald Trump har et mildest talt dårligt forhold til, og i juli sidste år blev hun fyret.
Mandag har en føderal dommer afgjort, at fyringen var ulovlig.
Det skriver AP.
'Kom fra Washington'
Efter sin fyring sidste sommer sagsøgte Maurene Comey det amerikanske justitsministerium. Hun hævdede, at fyringen dels var i strid med magtens tredeling og dels var i strid med punkter i henholdsvis det første og det femte forfatningstillæg. 
Comey hævdede i øvrigt, at fyringen skyldtes, at hun var James Comeys datter.
Ifølge NBC News har Comey forklaret, at den eneste begrundelse, hun fik for fyringen, var, at 'den kom fra Washington', hvilket senere blev bekræftet af Justitsministeriet, som oplyste, at ordren kom fra daværende justitsminister Pam Bondi.
Trump-regeringen argumenterede for, at fyringen af Comey levede op til reglerne, fordi føderale anklagere udøver præsidentens 'afgørende og forebyggende' beføjelser.
Dette såvel som flere andre argumenter afviste dommer Jesse M. Furman, som i sidste ende vurderede, at fyringen var i strid med blandt andet magtens tredeling og det femte forfatningstillæg.
Dommeren vedtog, at Comey skulle have udbetalt løn for perioden fra fyringen frem til december, hvor hun fik et nyt job.
I sin tid som anklager var Maurene Comey involveret i store amerikanske retssager. Blandt andet var hun involveret i sagerne mod rapperen Sean 'Diddy' Combs, Jeffrey Epstein og Epsteins partner Ghislaine Maxwell.
Artiklen fortsætter under billedet ...
Flere fyringer
Maurene Comey er ikke den eneste anklager, der er blevet fyret af Trump-administrationen. I februar beskrev blandt andre CBS News, at justitsministeriet havde pålagt Washingtons øverste anklager, Edward Martin, at fyre fire anklagere, der havde fået til opgave at efterforske stormen på Kongressen 6. januar.
Maurene Comeys far har ligeledes fået sparket af Donald Trump.
Det skete tilbage i 2017, og Trump-administrationen tilskrev selv fyringen Comeys håndtering af en efterforskning af den tidligere præsidentkandidat Hillary Clinton. Her skulle FBI undersøge, om Clinton havde kompromitteret den nationale sikkerhed ved at bruge en privat mailserver i sin tid som udenrigsminister under Barack Obama.
I 2016 udtalte Comey, at sagen burde lukkes, men 11 dage før valget blev sagen genåbnet. Det fik mange demokrater, herunder Clinton selv, til at beskylde Comey for at have kostet hende valgsejren.
Demokraterne har derimod beskyldt Trump-administrationen for at have fyret Comey, fordi FBI havde iværksat en efterforskning af formodede bånd mellem Rusland og Trumps præsidentkampagne.
Voldsom kritik
Fyringen medførte en voldsom bølge af kritik. Flere sammenlignede fyringen med 'The Saturday Night Massacre', som er et historisk punkt i amerikansk politik, hvor præsident Nixon under Watergate-skandalen fyrede anklageren i sagen Archibald Cox.
Selvom fyringen skete for ni år siden, har Trumps had til Comey varet ved.
Tidligere på året blev Comey således tiltalt for at have truet Donald Trump på livet på alternativ vis. I maj sidste år lagde den tidligere FBI-boss således et billede op på sociale medier, hvor noget så uskyldigt som muslingeskaller dannede talformationen '8647'.
Tallet 86 kan nemlig tolkes som slang for, at man vil skille sig af med noget, og da Donald Trump er den 47. præsident i USA, mente man, at der kunne rejses tiltale for dødstrusler mod præsidenten. I september sidste år forsøgte Trump-administrationen også at rejse tiltale mod Comey, men denne blev afvist af en føderal dommer.
Så sent som mandag aften dansk tid er det kommet frem, at James Comey for tredje gang er kommet under anklage. Denne gang er han blevet sigtet for at have videregivet oplysninger om forsvaret samt for sammensværgelse om at videregive oplysninger om forsvaret. Det skriver NBC News.

sources.news_title: Judge rules Trump DOJ ‘unlawfully’ fired Maurene Comey
sources.text:
A federal judge in New York on Monday ruled against President Donald Trump and the Justice Department over the firing of Maurene Comey, daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from the Manhattan U.S. attorney’s office.
Judge Jesse Furman said Comey’s termination violated civil service rules.
“Yes, the Attorney General is authorized by law to remove an AUSA. But the Attorney General (and anyone to whom the Attorney General delegates that authority) is also limited by law, namely the CSRA, to do so only in a particular manner and only for certain reasons,” the judge wrote.
Furman ordered Maurene Comey, who most recently led the prosecution of Sean “Diddy” Combs, reinstated with back pay.
In addition to calling her termination unlawful, Furman decided Trump and the DOJ violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and Maurene Comey’s due process rights.
“The Department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course,” a DOJ spokesperson told ABC News.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York declined to comment.
ABC News has reached out to Maurene Comey for comment.
Furman’s ruling outlines that Maurene Comey’s reinstatement applies from the date of her termination in July of 2025 until December, when she effectively resigned from her role by accepting a new job in the private sector.
In ordering Maurene Comey’s reinstatement, Furman rejected what he described as the Trump administration’s “sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority.”
The Trump administration had argued that not only was Maurene Comey’s firing lawful under federal statute, but that the laws protecting civil servants were also an unconstitutional intrusion into Trump’s authority.
“The question at the heart of this case is whether these limitations on the removal of Assistant United States Attorneys are consistent with Article II and the constitutional separation of powers,” Judge Furman wrote.
To make its argument, the DOJ pointed to the Supreme Court’s decision in Trump v. Slaughter — where the justices effectively supercharged presidential power by greenlighting the firing of the leaders of independent federal agencies — and the Trump v. United States immunity case
“On their view, AUSAs who represent the United States in criminal cases in court exercise prosecutorial and investigatory functions that fall squarely within the President’s ‘conclusive and preclusive’ powers,” Furman wrote. “Accordingly, they argue, the President — and, by extension, the heads of departments appointed by the President — must have the power to remove such AUSAs for any reason or no reason at all.”
But Furman rejected the DOJ’s interpretation of the legal precedent, pointing to decades of other cases which affirm the legal protections for line prosecutors. He also noted that neither case cited by the DOJ applies to inferior officers or “supports their sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority.”
“Defendants’ argument is contrary to an unbroken line of Supreme Court decisions dating back almost two centuries, and the Supreme Court itself has not formally overruled any of those decisions. That is sufficient, in itself, to reject the argument,” wrote Judge Furman.
To accept the DOJ’s argument, Furman wrote, would “unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”
Maurene Comey was an assistant U.S. attorney who successfully prosecuted Ghislaine Maxwell, the former associate of sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and multiple gang members before the split verdict last year in the trial of Combs, who was convicted of a prostitution-related charge but acquitted of more serious charges.
She was also involved in the office’s case against Epstein, who died by suicide in 2019 at New York City’s Metropolitan Correctional Center while he was awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.
Trump fired James Comey during his first term in office after Comey announced publicly that Trump’s 2016 campaign was being investigated over potential ties to Russia.
Prior to Maurene Comey’s firing, Trump privately vented about having a Comey work in his administration, sources previously told ABC News.
Earlier this year, Furman blocked the Justice Department’s attempt to move Maurene Comey’s lawsuit over her firing as a federal prosecutor out of court.
The Justice Department argued at the time that her case belongs before the Merit Systems Protection Board and not in federal district court.
Furman decided the case belongs with him because Maurene Comey was fired pursuant to the president’s executive authority and not the usual procedures for civil servants.
“Maurene Comey was, by all accounts, an exemplary Assistant United States Attorney. In her nearly ten years working at the United States Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, she was assigned some of the country’s highest profile cases, and she consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike,” the judge’s opinion in April said.
The DOJ, in court filings, has characterized Comey’s case as routine.
“A federal employee’s claims that removal from federal service was arbitrary and capricious or conducted in a manner that did not provide the process to which they contend they were due is not a novel issue,” government attorneys previously said.
Following her termination last year, Maurene Comey told colleagues in a farewell email that she was fired as a federal prosecutor without being told a reason but urged them not to succumb to the “fear” she said her firing could cause.
“If a career prosecutor can be fired without reason, fear may seep into the decision of those who remain,” Comey said in her email, a copy of which was obtained by ABC News. “Do not let that happen.”

sources.news_title: 'The President is not above the law': Judge finds DOJ illegally fired James Comey's daughter
sources.text:
The Trump administration illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of ex-FBI Director and Trump critic James Comey, as a Justice Department prosecutor, a judge ruled Monday, sharply rebuking the administration’s authority to terminate career federal employees it dislikes.
The ruling is tailored to Maurene Comey but its import stretches beyond her case, repudiating the claim of President Donald Trump’s administration that the Constitution permits such firings for any reason. Administration officials have cited that belief repeatedly in a sweeping purge of the federal workforce.
Comey, an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was fired in July 2025 despite her work on some of the nation’s highest-profile cases and consistently receiving “the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike,” Judge Jesse M. Furman found.
After her firing, Comey sued the Justice Department and others, saying her termination violated the constitutional separation of powers, the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.
She asserted that she was fired because she was the daughter of James Comey, whom Trump has long viewed as an enemy, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both, the judge noted.
Furman rejected the government’s claim that Comey could be fired because federal prosecutors exercise the president’s “conclusive and preclusive” powers.
He also said the government’s claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.”
Furman added: “Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”
The firing violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, the judge ruled. He reserved judgment on Comey’s First Amendment claim pending further arguments, though he said he was inclined to dismiss it because it was largely moot since she is now in private practice and no longer seeks actual reinstatement.
Furman, who was nominated to the bench in 2011 by then-Democratic President Barack Obama, granted Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20 to “make her whole” and ensure that she doesn’t suffer adverse employment consequences for the “unlawful termination.”
In a statement, the Justice Department said it “disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course.”
Comey’s lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling.
“This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law,” they said in a statement. “As the Court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power ‘would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.’ This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law.”
Comey was fired two weeks after leading the prosecution of music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs, which ended in a conviction on prostitution-related charges but an acquittal on others. She also worked on the sex trafficking prosecutions of Jeffrey Epstein, the financier who killed himself in jail a month after his arrest in 2019, and Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime confidant Ghislaine Maxwell, who was convicted in 2021 and is serving a 20-year prison sentence.
The Justice Department during the Trump administration has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration’s agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits.
The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father’s longtime adversarial relationship with Trump.
The president fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican’s successful 2016 campaign for the White House. Trump in the years since has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen.
An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47,” a case he has sought to dismiss that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.
___
Tucker and Durkin reported from Washington.

Oct. 26 2026, Published 5:20 p.m. ET
President Donald Trump's Justice Department has been dealt a stunning legal blow after a federal judge ruled the administration illegally fired veteran prosecutor Maurene Comey, who helped bring cases against Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, RadarOnline.com can reveal.
According to a 55-page court ruling filed Monday, October 26, and obtained by Radar, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman determined that Comey's July 2025 dismissal violated federal law and constitutional protections — while court filings revealed that former Attorney General Pam Bondi personally directed her removal.
The bombshell ruling details how the administration sought to justify Comey's termination through sweeping claims of presidential authority.
Bondi's Role Exposed in Court Documents
In court filings, government attorneys acknowledged that Comey was removed at Bondi's direction, with Executive Office for United States Attorneys Director John Hakes signing the termination memorandum.
The administration subsequently attempted to defend the firing through a May 2026 memorandum issued by then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, purporting to ratify the earlier decision.
But Furman rejected the government's expansive interpretation of executive power, finding that federal prosecutors cannot simply be stripped of statutory employment protections.
The judge warned that accepting the administration's position would undermine the constitutional balance between Congress and the presidency.
Epstein Prosecutor Fired Without Explanation
Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, spent nearly a decade prosecuting major federal criminal cases in Manhattan.
Her assignments included the investigations involving Epstein, Maxwell, disgraced music mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs and former Democratic Senator Bob Menendez.
Despite receiving outstanding performance evaluations between 2019 and 2024, Comey was abruptly dismissed in July 2025 without an explanation.
She later alleged that her termination stemmed from Trump's longstanding hostility toward her father, whom the president fired as FBI director in 2017.
However, the court did not determine that political retaliation motivated her dismissal.
Judge Orders Back Pay After Illegal Dismissal
Furman concluded that the Justice Department violated the Civil Service Reform Act, which requires legally sufficient cause and procedural safeguards before covered federal employees can be removed.
The ruling also found violations of Comey's Fifth Amendment due process rights and the Administrative Procedure Act.
In a significant victory for the former prosecutor, Furman ordered her retroactively reinstated and awarded back pay covering July 16 through December 20, 2025, when she accepted another position.

Trump Administration Vows to Appeal
Comey's attorneys celebrated the ruling as a victory for government accountability and constitutional checks on presidential power.
The Justice Department, however, rejected the decision, with a spokesperson confirming that the administration intends to appeal.
The ruling raises broader questions about the administration's authority to dismiss career prosecutors, particularly those connected to politically sensitive investigations.
For now, the decision represents a significant legal defeat for Trump's Justice Department — and places Bondi's involvement in Comey's controversial dismissal squarely in the spotlight.

US judge says firing of daughter of former FBI director unlawful
Former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey sued the US Department of Justice, alleging she was fired because of her father, James Comey’s, criticism of US President Donald Trump or because of her perceived political beliefs.
NEW YORK: A US judge ruled on Monday (Oct 26) that the firing of former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, the daughter of Donald Trump foe James Comey, was unlawful and she should be reinstated.
Comey, whose father briefly served as FBI director during Trump's first White House term, was summarily dismissed in July 2025 as an assistant US attorney in Manhattan.
Comey filed suit against the Department of Justice in federal court claiming she had been dismissed "solely or substantially" because of her father's criticism of Trump or "because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs."
In ruling against the Department of Justice, District Judge Jesse Furman said Comey, an assistant US attorney (AUSA) in the Southern District of New York, had been deprived of her due process rights.
"Yes, the Attorney General is authorised by law to remove an AUSA," Furman said. "But the Attorney General ... is also limited by law ... to do so only in a particular manner and only for certain reasons."
Comey was involved in a number of prominent cases while serving as a prosecutor in Manhattan, including those brought against music producer Sean "Diddy" Combs and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
She also prosecuted Ghislaine Maxwell, the only former Epstein associate who was criminally charged in connection with his activities. Epstein died in prison before coming to trial in what was determined to be a suicide.
Since taking office, Trump has taken a number of punitive measures against his perceived enemies, purging government officials deemed to be disloyal, targeting law firms involved in past cases against him and pulling federal funding from universities.
James Comey, an outspoken critic of Trump, was indicted in April for allegedly threatening the Republican president in an Instagram post that showed the numbers "8647" spelled out in seashells.
The Trump Justice Department has claimed that "8647" constitutes a threat to the president - "86" meaning to kill and "47" a reference to Trump being the 47th president. Comey has denied threatening the president's life.
Trump fired Comey in 2017 as the then-FBI chief was leading an investigation into whether any members of the president's campaign had colluded with Moscow to sway the 2016 election, in which the Republican beat Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton.

Obama judge orders Trump DOJ to retroactively reinstate Comey's daughter as federal prosecutor
Another Obama appointee has weighed in on the Trump administration's personnel decisions.
An Obama-appointed federal judge ruled on Monday that while Trump's attorney general and those with the delegated responsibility are "authorized by law" to fire a federal prosecutor, the way in which the daughter of disgraced ex-FBI Director James Comey was fired last year was unlawful.
Maurene Comey served as an assistant U.S. attorney in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York for nearly a decade and was involved in the prosecutions of Sean "Diddy" Combs, convicted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein, and child sex trafficker Ghislaine Maxwell.
'This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances.'
Francey Hakes, the director of the Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys, notified Comey on July 16, 2025, that "pursuant to Article II of the United States Constitution and the laws of the United States," her employment with the Justice Department had been terminated.
In September 2025, Comey sued the Trump administration, alleging that her termination was "unlawful and unconstitutional" and "politically motivated" — the result of her connection to James Comey and/or "her perceived political affiliation and beliefs." According to her complaint, she was removable only for cause under the Civil Service Reform Act.
The government argued that:
- Comey was removable at-will under Article II by the attorney general "because plaintiff in her duties as an assistant United States attorney exercised the president’s conclusive and preclusive executive authority";
- "Congress has by statute explicitly authorized the attorney general to remove assistant United States attorneys"; and
- that statute "contains no restrictions on the attorney general's removal powers."

U.S. District Court Judge Jesse Furman, an appointee of former President Barack Obama, evidently was not swayed by the government's arguments. He ruled on Monday that Comey's "removal was not authorized by any statute; to the contrary, it violated the CSRA."
While conceding that the attorney general can remove an AUSA, Furman wrote that "the attorney general (and anyone to whom the attorney general delegates that authority) is also limited by law, namely the CSRA, to do so only in a particular manner and only for certain reasons."
"The Court holds that Comey is entitled to judgment as a matter of law on her central claims that she was terminated in violation of the constitutional separation of powers and federal law," continued the Obama judge.
Furman ordered Comey's retroactive reinstatement and backpay effective from her termination in July through Dec. 20, 2025, when the ex-prosecutor apparently found a new job.
Comey's lawyers said in a joint statement, "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."
"As the Court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation’s constitutional system,'" continued the lawyers. "This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the president is not above the law."
The White House referred Blaze News to the following statement from the Justice Department's rapid response account: "The Department disagrees with this decision, which obstructs President Trump’s constitutional authority to fire individuals who wield executive power on his behalf. We intend to appeal the decision in due course."

US court rules daughter of Trump critic James Comey was illegally fired

A United States judge has ruled that former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey was illegally fired by the administration of President Donald Trump.
US District Judge Jesse Furman said on Monday that the Trump administration had overstepped the boundaries of executive authority when it fired so-called “inferior officers” without cause.
He rejected the administration’s position that the president had the power to undertake such firings, regardless of the protections implemented by Congress.

The judge ruled that Comey's dismissal violated the constitutional separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act, and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights. He found that the removal also breached protections under the Civil Service Reform Act.

(CNN) — A federal judge on Monday found the Justice Department’s firing of Maurene Comey, a former federal prosecutor who presided over several high-profile cases including those of Jeffrey Epstein and Sean “Diddy” Combs, was unconstitutional.
Comey, an assistant US attorney for the Southern District of New York for nearly a decade, was fired in July 2025. She filed a lawsuit claiming the firing was in retaliation because her father is former FBI Director James Comey, a vocal opponent of President Donald Trump.
Until she was fired, Comey received accolades from her supervisors and was frequently tapped for some of the office’s biggest cases. DOJ, in its arguments, acknowledged Comey was not fired for cause or due to her performance.
Judge Jesse Furman said the Justice Department’s firing violated the separation of powers clause of the US Constitution, which places limits on how certain federal employees can be fired. He also found it violated the Civil Service Reform Act, which guards the process by which federal employees can be removed.
“Yes, the Attorney General is authorized by law to remove an AUSA. But the Attorney General (and anyone to whom the Attorney General delegates that authority) is also limited by law, namely the CSRA, to do so only in a particular manner and only for certain reasons. The Justice Department had argued the attorney general exercises the president’s powers and could not be limited by Congress.
Furman said DOJ’s argument that Congress cannot dictate how federal employees are removed would upend two centuries of Supreme Court decisions. To agree with DOJ would “risk a return to the spoils system that Congress has sought to end since the nineteenth century,” he wrote.

“This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law,” Maurene Comey’s legal team said in a statement. “As the Court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power ‘would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.’”

Furman rejected that position, finding that Comey’s firing violated the Civil Service Reform Act, the landmark 1978 statute that shields federal employees from certain forms of arbitrary termination. The administration, he wrote, was seeking to “upend” established precedent permitting Congress to regulate the removal of so-called inferior officers.
“Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system,” Furman wrote.
Comey’s attorneys described the ruling as a “hard-earned victory” not only for their client but also for federal workers across the government.
“As the Court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power ‘would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.’ This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law,” lawyers Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan said in a statement.
A Justice Department spokesperson said the agency “disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course.”
Comey joined the Manhattan U.S. Attorney’s Office in 2015 and worked on several prominent criminal prosecutions, including cases involving Sean “Diddy” Combs, Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell and former Democratic Sen. Robert Menendez.

sources.news_title: Trump's Firing Of Prosecutor Maurene Comey Was Unlawful, Judge Rules
sources.text:
NEW YORK, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The abrupt firing of Maurene Comey as a federal prosecutor by President Donald Trump’s administration was unlawful, a US judge ruled on Monday in a victory for the eldest daughter of former FBI director and longtime Trump adversary James Comey.
Maurene Comey, who brought criminal cases against Jeffrey Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell and music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs during a tenure at the Manhattan US Attorney’s office that began in 2015, was fired by Trump’s Justice Department in July 2025. Her dismissal came a few months after the Republican president began his second term in office.
In a lawsuit against the administration, she alleged that she was fired because of who her father was, in violation of federal laws prohibiting firing civil servants for political reasons and guaranteeing federal employees due process in employment disputes.
The case was seen as a test of whether the administration can swiftly fire career prosecutors like Comey who were not politically appointed and whose careers tend to span both Republican and Democratic presidential administrations.
Executive Branch Authority
In court papers, the Justice Department argued that prosecutors like Comey are subject to removal without cause by the president or the attorney general because they are delegated a high degree of executive authority when they represent the federal government in court in criminal cases.
In siding with Comey, US District Judge Jesse Furman said centuries of legal precedent affirmed the authority of Congress to place limits on the executive branch’s ability to remove so-called “inferior officers.”
“To accept defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation’s constitutional system,” wrote Furman, who is based in Manhattan and was appointed by Democratic former President Barack Obama.
The judge granted her request to retroactively reinstate her as a prosecutor through December 2025 so she could get back pay and qualify for retirement benefits.
The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
During his second term, Trump has sought to expand his authority over federal government entities that have historically experienced varying degrees of independence from the White House, including the Justice Department. His critics accuse him of using criminal prosecutions to punish political foes, including James Comey, and reward allies.
James Comey Hit With Charges
Trump in 2017 during his first term fired James Comey, who at the time was leading an FBI investigation into contacts between Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and Russians. Comey in 2018 called Trump morally “unfit to be president.” Trump defeated Democrat Hillary Clinton in the 2016 election.
Trump’s Justice Department last year charged James Comey with lying to Congress about authorizing leaks to the news media, one of the highest-profile instances of the Trump administration using law enforcement to target perceived political enemies. Comey pleaded not guilty, and the case was dismissed after a judge found that the federal prosecutor who secured the charges had not been lawfully appointed.
James Comey has since been charged in a separate federal case with threatening Trump by posting a photograph of seashells arranged to show the numbers “86 47.” Comey has pleaded not guilty. The number 86 is a slang term originating in the restaurant industry that can mean to “get rid of” or throw someone out, while 47 may refer to Trump, the 47th US president.
James Comey has called the cases against him vindictive prosecutions motivated by Trump’s animosity.
In February, Maurene Comey was hired as a partner at law firm Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler.
(Reporting by Luc Cohen in New York; Editing by David Gaffen and Will Dunham)

In his opinion, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman, appointed by former President Barack Obama, said Comey’s firing violated the Civil Service Reform Act and rejected the DOJ’s claim that the president holds the ability to fire federal prosecutors under Article II of the Constitution.
Furman said the defendant’s claims that presidential power supersedes the right to due process “flies in the face of over forty years of consistent policy and practice of the Executive Branch.”
“Defendants’ contention that recent Supreme Court decisions have fatally undermined that precedent is not one that this Court, as a lower court, may accept,” Furman said. “It is also without merit. sources.news_title: Trump Administration Unlawfully Fired Epstein Prosecutor Maurene Comey, Court Rules
Judge rules Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director, was unlawfully fired by Trump administration – WTOP News
sources.text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The Trump administration illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of ex-FBI Director and Trump critic James Comey, as a Justice Department prosecutor, a judge ruled Monday in a sharp rebuke of the administration’s authority to terminate career federal employees it dislikes.
The ruling is tailored to Maurene Comey but its import stretches beyond her case, repudiating the claim of President Donald Trump’s administration that the Constitution permits such firings for any reason. Administration officials have cited that belief repeatedly in a sweeping purge of the federal workforce.
Comey, an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was fired in July 2025 despite consistently receiving “the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike,” Judge Jesse M. Furman found.
The judge said her firing violated laws passed by Congress that were intended to abolish the spoils system, under which newly elected presidents regularly purged government workers and replaced them with loyalists.
Furman’s decision didn’t address the validity of Comey’s claim that she was fired because she is the daughter of James Comey, whom Trump has long viewed as an enemy.
Trump fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican’s successful 2016 campaign for the White House. Trump in the years since has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen.
Hours after Furman’s ruling Monday, unsealed court filings showed that the Justice Department had quietly brought another criminal case against James Comey, accusing him of leaking classified information.
Furman, who was nominated to the bench in 2011 by then-Democratic President Barack Obama, granted Maurene Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20, 2025, when she began a new, private-sector job.
In a statement, the Justice Department said it disagreed with this decision and would appeal.
Comey’s lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling.
“This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law,” they said in a statement. “This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law.”
Comey was fired two weeks after leading the prosecution of music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs, which ended in a conviction on prostitution-related charges but an acquittal on others. She also worked on the sex trafficking prosecutions of Jeffrey Epstein, the financier who killed himself in jail a month after his arrest in 2019, and Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime confidant Ghislaine Maxwell, who was convicted in 2021 and is serving a 20-year prison sentence.
The Justice Department during the Trump administration has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration’s agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits.
The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father’s longtime adversarial relationship with Trump.
An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47,” a case he has sought to dismiss that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.
In his ruling on Maurene Comey’s termination, Furman said the Justice Department’s claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.”
Furman added: “Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”
He didn’t rule on Comey’s claim that her firing violated her free speech rights, though he said he was inclined to dismiss it because she is now in private practice and no longer seeks reinstatement to her old job.

Tucker and Durkin reported from Washington.

sources.text:
A federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice's firing last year of New York federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was unlawful.
Judge Jesse Furman, in his ruling, also granted Maurene Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay as an assistant U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York from her termination on July 16, 2025, through Dec. 20, 2025, when the judge inferred she accepted another job.
The DOJ said it would appeal Furman's ruling in which the judge rejected the department's arguments that the attorney general had authority to dismiss Comey without cause. The case is in in U.S. District Court in Manhattan.
Comey's lawyers, in a statement, said, "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."
"As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system,'" the lawyers said. "This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law."
Before her termination, Comey was involved in a series of high-profile federal prosecutions, including ones against the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean "Diddy" Combs.
Her lawsuit against the DOJ argued that her termination violated federal law and the Constitution and stemmed from President Donald Trump's longstanding animus toward her father, whom Trump had fired as FBI director in 2017.
James Comey is currently under federal indictment that accuses him of threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells forming the number "86 47." His attorneys are seeking to have that case tossed out.
James Comey, who denies any wrongdoing, previously had another federal indictment against him filed by the DOJ under Trump dismissed.
Maurene Comey's suit said the DOJ did not give "any explanation whatsoever for terminating Ms. Comey," and, "In truth, there is no legitimate explanation."
"Rather, Defendants fired Ms. Comey solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B. Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both," the suit said.
Furman, in his ruling for Comey, referenced that claim, but his decision was based on other grounds.
The judge rejected the DOJ's arguments that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi could remove a federal prosecutor "at will" and without cause and that current Attorney General Todd Blanche could ratify that act after the fact as he did in May as acting attorney general.
Furman also rejected the DOJ's argument that even if the Civil Service Reform Act requires removal of a prosecutor for cause, an attorney general's firing of her constituted an implicit determination that she was removed "for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service."
"The Court need not dwell long on Defendants' second statutory argument justifying Comey's removal," Furman said, referring to that claim.
"That is because the argument borders on frivolous."
The judge noted that Comey was fired despite having had excellent performance reviews.
"Comey's supervisors and peers consistently lauded her work, describing her as a 'brilliant lawyer and a gifted supervisor,' 'the lawyer the office turns to when legal excellence is a must,' and 'an outstanding AUSA in every respect' with 'judgment, work product, and courtroom advocacy [that are] among the finest in the country,'" Furman wrote.
The DOJ admitted that Comey's termination "was not 'for cause' and was not based on her
performance," Furman noted.
In addition, the judge said, the DOJ's argument that Comey's termination was lawful ignored parts of the Civil Service Reform Act, which "required that Comey be given advance written notice (subject to certain exceptions not relevant here); 'a reasonable time' to respond orally and in writing; representation; and 'a written decision and the specific reasons therefor at the earliest practicable date.'"
"Defendants concede, as they must, that Comey was not afforded these procedural protections," the judge said.
Furman also said the DOJ all but admitted that its argument that the attorney general had power to fire Comey under Article II of the U.S. Constitution — which establishes the executive branch of government — sought "to overturn nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent."
"This Court, however, is bound to follow the Supreme Court's precedents unless and until the Supreme Court overturns them," Furman wrote.
The DOJ, in a statement, said, "The Department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."
That appeal would happen after Furman issues a final judgment in the case.
The judge reserved judgment on Comey's claim that her firing violated her First Amendment rights. Furman gave her until Nov. 9 to file arguments on why that claim should not be dismissed as moot given his order in her favor on other grounds.
CNBC has requested comment on the ruling from the White House.
Comey, in a note to colleagues at the U.S. Attorney's Office after she was fired, wrote, "If a career prosecutor can be fired without reason, fear may seep into the decisions of those who remain."
"Fear is the tool of a tyrant, wielded to suppress independent thought. Instead of fear, let this moment fuel the fire that already burns in the heart of this place," she wrote. "A fire of righteous indignation at abuses of power. Of commitment to seek justice for victims."

In a 55-page order, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman granted Maurene Comey’s request for retroactive reinstatement and back pay.
Furman, a Barack Obama appointee in the Southern District of New York, criticized the government’s defense of her termination as one that “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.” The second Trump administration has embraced unrestricted removal power by the executive branch, which Furman said was unconstitutional in this case.
“Indeed, to accept defendant’s argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation’s constitutional system,” the judge wrote.
Maurene Comey sued the Trump administration in September 2025, claiming the government fired her that summer for politically motivated reasons. A veteran federal prosecutor, she was involved in some of the biggest cases the Southern District of New York has seen in recent years, including prosecutions against rap mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs and pedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein.
She claims in her lawsuit the government gave “no legitimate explanation” for her firing. She says she believes she was terminated “solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B. Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both.”
Furman found the government improperly relied on Article II executive powers as the sole justification for Maurene Comey’s termination, despite her having too junior a role in the Department of Justice for that to apply.
“In purporting to fire Comey pursuant to Article II and the laws of the United States, defendants invented a new and expansive theory of executive power,” the judge wrote. “And they have also utilized that theory to remove other executive branch employees who have long held protections from removal.”
Furman added that the attorney general is authorized to remove an assistant U.S. attorney by the Civil Service Reform Act only “in a particular manner and for certain reasons.”
“And Comey’s removal indisputably violated the CSRA,” he found.
Following Furman’s ruling, Maurene Comey is entitled to retroactive back pay from July 16, 2025, the date of her termination, to Dec. 20, 2025, when she started a new job on Patterson Belknap’s white-collar defense team.
“This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants and to all fighting for the rule of law,” her lawyers Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan said in a joint statement to Courthouse News. “As the court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power ‘would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation’s constitutional system.’ This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: The president is not above the law.”
A DOJ spokesperson said the department “disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course.”
Despite nearly a decade passing since he last ran the FBI, James Comey continues to be one of President Donald Trump’s top political targets. He’s being federally charged by Trump’s DOJ for posting a photo on Instagram of seashells forming “86 47” — a slogan prosecutors say was a threat on Trump’s life.
Their political clash dates back to Trump’s first term, when James Comey refused to shield Trump from the FBI’s investigations into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. Trump fired him in 2017, acknowledging in subsequent interviews the Russia probe played a major role in that decision.
James Comey has since become one of the president’s most fervent critics. He chastised Trump in his 2018 memoir, likening him to a mob boss and suggesting he was unfit to lead the United States.

Judge rules Maurene Comey was unlawfully fired from federal prosecutor role
Washington — A federal judge on Monday found that the Justice Department unlawfully fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from her post as a federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York.
U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman said in a 55-page decision that Comey’s removal violated the constitutional separation of powers and federal law. The judge retroactively reinstated Comey to her role as a federal prosecutor and ordered the Trump administration to provide her back pay from the date of her firing in July 2025 through Dec. 20, when she accepted a different job.
Comey’s lawsuit was one of several filed by former government employees who were fired without cause that tested the limits of the president’s power to fire federal officials.
The Trump administration had argued that Article II of the Constitution gives the president unrestricted removal power, and said Congress could not limit the removal of federal prosecutors.
But in his decision, Furman ruled that Comey’s firing violated the Civil Service Reform Act, a landmark law enacted in 1978 that provides protections for federal workers. The Trump administration, he wrote, is attempting to “upend” long-settled case law allowing Congress to regulate the removal of so-called inferior officers.
“Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system,” Furman wrote.
Comey’s legal team cheered the decision as a “hard-earned victory” for her and all civil servants.
“As the Court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power ‘would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.’ This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law,” lawyers Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan said in a statement.
A Justice Department spokesperson said it “disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course.”
Comey had served as a federal prosecutor in Manhattan since 2015, handling high-profile criminal cases against figures including Sean “Diddy” Combs, Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell and former Democratic Sen. Robert Menendez.
In a letter to her former colleagues at the time of her dismissal, Comey said she was “summarily fired via memo” by the Justice Department’s headquarters in Washington, and was not given a reason for her termination.
The letter she received stated, “Pursuant to Article II of the United States Constitution and the laws of the United States, your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately.”
It was initially unclear who made the decision to oust Comey, but in May, the Trump administration said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi “directed” her removal, and her successor, Todd Blanche, “ratified” her termination.
Comey sued the Justice Department over her firing last year, alleging she had probably been fired because President Trump dislikes her father, who has been indicted twice during the second Trump administration. One of the criminal cases was tossed out, and James Comey has denied wrongdoing in the second.
“Ms. Comey’s termination — without cause, without advance notice, and without any opportunity to contest it — was unlawful and unconstitutional,” Comey’s attorneys wrote in their complaint.
The Trump administration attempted to dismiss the lawsuit on the grounds that Comey was required to bring her claims before the Merit Systems Protection Board, the agency tasked with adjudicating appeals from federal employees regarding adverse actions taken against them, but Furman denied the government’s motion and allowed the case to continue.
Furman found that because Comey’s firing rested on Article II of the Constitution — not a federal law governing the civil service — the federal court had jurisdiction to hear the case.
In court filings, the Justice Department admitted that Comey had received a rating of “outstanding” on her performance reviews from 2019 through 2024, but said that her firing had been carried out under legal authority Congress granted to the attorney general to fire assistant U.S. attorneys.
In defending Comey’s firing, the Trump administration relied, in part, on the Supreme Court’s June decision allowing the president to fire members of certain independent agencies without cause. In that case, the high court overturned a more than 90-year-old decision that allowed Congress to restrict the president’s ability to fire officials from multimember agencies at will.
But Furman said the Justice Department’s argument amounted to a “sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority.”

Furman also rejected the DOJ’s argument that even if the Civil Service Reform Act requires removal of a prosecutor for cause, an attorney general’s firing of her constituted an implicit determination that she was removed “for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service.”
“The Court need not dwell long on Defendants’ second statutory argument justifying
Comey’s removal,” Furman said, referring to that claim. “That is because the argument borders on frivolous.”
The judge noted that Comey was fired despite having had excellent performance reviews.
“Comey’s supervisors and peers consistently lauded her work, describing her as a

Furman also said the DOJ all but admitted that its argument that the attorney general had power to fire Comey under Article II of the Constitution sought “to overturn nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.”
